---
title: "Differential abundance"
---

Which protein groups change between conditions? This guide compares the three
IFNa-treated HepG2 samples with the three controls using `se` from
[Preparing data](preparing-data.html).

ProteoVaultR uses **limma** to fit a model for each protein group and share
variance information across groups to stabilize the tests. See the
[limma User's Guide](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/limma/inst/doc/usersguide.pdf)
for the statistical background.

```{r setup, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ProteoVaultR)
library(dplyr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
    dev.args = list(bg = "white")
)
data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROTEOVAULTR_DEMO_DIR", unset = "demo-data")
vault <- open_vault(
    file.path(data_dir, "hepg2_ifna-dia.proteovault.duckdb")
)
sample_info <- tibble::tribble(
    ~sample_name,   ~sample_id, ~condition,
    "Control_R1",  "Ctrl1",    "Control",
    "Control_R2",  "Ctrl2",    "Control",
    "Control_R3",  "Ctrl3",    "Control",
    "IFNa_12h_R1", "IFNa1",    "IFNa",
    "IFNa_12h_R2", "IFNa2",    "IFNa",
    "IFNa_12h_R3", "IFNa3",    "IFNa"
)
sample_info$condition <- factor(
    sample_info$condition, levels = c("Control", "IFNa")
)
vault <- set_sample_metadata(vault, sample_info)
se <- as_summarized_experiment(vault, method = "matrix")
close_vault(vault)
```

## 1. Choose the quantities

Here we use the imported DIA-NN matrix in the `quantity` assay, the default for
`fit_limma()`. Use the original intensity scale: the function applies log2 by
default, treats zeros as missing, and passes missing values to limma.

If you chose additional [normalization](normalization.html) or
[imputation](missing-values.html), use the corresponding object and select its
assay in the fitting call:

- For `se_genorm`, set `assay = "quantity_genorm_normalized"`.
- For `se_imputed`, set `assay = "quantity_imputed"`.

## 2. Define the comparison

The `condition` column contains `Control` and `IFNa`, in that order. The formula
below fits a mean for each condition, and the contrast specifies their difference:

```{r define-contrast}
design <- ~ 0 + condition
contrasts <- list_limma_contrasts(se, design)
contrasts
```

`IFNa_vs_Control` compares IFNa minus Control. Positive log2 fold changes mean
higher abundance in IFNa; a value of 1 means a twofold increase.
These are independent biological replicates, so the model does not pair samples
by their replicate numbers.

## 3. Fit the model and read the results

Fit the contrast, then preview ten groups ranked by adjusted p-value. We keep a
compact statistics table in `results`; `fit$results` retains all annotations.

```{r fit-model, warning=FALSE}
fit <- fit_limma(se, design = design, contrasts = contrasts)
results <- fit$results %>%
    select(feature_id, leading_gene_name, leading_protein_accession, logFC, P.Value, adj.P.Val)
results %>%
    arrange(adj.P.Val, P.Value) %>%
    head(10) %>%
    select(-feature_id) %>%
    mutate(across(c(P.Value, adj.P.Val), ~ formatC(.x, format = "e", digits = 2))) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Gene", "Leading protein", "Log2 fold change", "p-value", "Adjusted p-value"),
        digits = 2
    )
```

`logFC` gives the estimated log2 fold change. `P.Value` is the unadjusted p-value;
`adj.P.Val` applies the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment across protein groups in
this contrast. Each row still represents a protein group; the leading gene and
protein provide labels.

Here, `r sum(is.finite(results$P.Value))` of `r nrow(results)` groups have a finite
p-value. Groups without enough measurements to estimate the comparison can have
missing statistics.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Two different questions:** Identification FDR concerns which peptides or
proteins were identified. The adjusted p-values here concern differences in
abundance between conditions.
:::

## 4. Plot the comparison

### 4.1. Inspect the p-value distribution

```{r pvalue-histogram, fig.alt="Histogram of raw limma p-values for the HepG2 IFNa-versus-Control comparison."}
plot_limma_pvalue_histogram(fit)
```

The histogram summarizes raw p-values across protein groups. An excess near zero
can reflect a treatment response; interpret the pattern alongside sample QC and
the experimental design.

### 4.2. Inspect effect sizes and significance

```{r volcano, fig.alt="Volcano plot of log2 fold change against negative log10 BH-adjusted p-value for IFNa versus Control."}
plot_limma_volcano(fit)
```

Groups on the right have higher abundance in IFNa; those on the left have lower
abundance. Higher points have smaller adjusted p-values. By default, colored
points meet the adjusted p-value cutoff of 0.05. Groups with missing statistics
are omitted.

## 5. Select and save results

For example, select groups with an adjusted p-value at or below 0.05:

```{r select-results}
significant <- results %>% filter(adj.P.Val <= 0.05)
nrow(significant)
```

Consider effect sizes and biological context alongside this threshold. `results`
still contains every fitted row, including groups with missing statistics.

To save the unfiltered statistics table locally:

```{r export-csv, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(results, "IFNa_vs_Control-results.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

To preserve the full fitted object, including its model, settings, and
protein-group annotations:

```{r save-fit, eval=FALSE}
saveRDS(fit, "IFNa_vs_Control-fit.rds")
```

sample quantities, precursor profiles, and sequence coverage.
